summary: Defines terminology for discussing network mobility (NEMO), where a whole network moves and changes its attachment point to the Internet. The terms are meant to be used consistently in the NEMO issues and solution requirements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4885 defines terms for describing a whole network that moves through the Internet. It helps readers distinguish its routers, devices, nested networks, and kinds of mobility support.

questions: what is a nested mobile network
subtitle: A common vocabulary for networks whose router changes its point of attachment.

tldr.problem: When a router carrying an entire network moves, sessions between devices in that network and the Internet can break. Researchers need shared terms to describe the components and mobility cases.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines architectural roles and terminology for nested networks, multihoming, home-network models, and network mobility support.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4885 is an Informational terminology document, not a protocol. It identifies RFC 3963 as the specified solution for NEMO Basic Support.

today: RFC 4885 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; RFC 3963 is the solution it identifies for NEMO Basic Support.

sections.title: Network Mobility
sections.content:
Network mobility concerns an entire network whose router changes its point of attachment to the Internet. The move changes the network's reachability, and without mobility support, existing sessions between its nodes and the wider Internet cannot be maintained.

The RFC defines terminology for discussing the problem, design goals, and proposed solutions. It uses NEMO for either a network that is mobile or the concept of network mobility, depending on context.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile network moves as a unit when its router changes the network connection it uses. RFC 4885 supplies terms for discussing what happens to the network and its sessions.

sections.title: Components of a Mobile Network
sections.content:
A mobile network contains one or more mobile IP subnets and connects to the Internet through one or more mobile routers (MRs). A mobile router forwards traffic between the network and an access router. Its egress interfaces face the home or foreign link; its ingress interfaces face links inside the mobile network.

A Mobile Network Prefix identifies the network in IP addresses used by its nodes. A Mobile Network Node can be any host or router located inside the network, temporarily or permanently. A Correspondent Node is a node communicating with one or more of those mobile-network nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile router connects the moving network to the Internet and forwards traffic to and from its internal links. Nodes inside the network use addresses containing its mobile-network prefix.

sections.title: Node Roles and Nested Networks
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes three kinds of mobile-network nodes. A Local Fixed Node belongs to the network but cannot change attachment while maintaining sessions. A Local Mobile Node can move while maintaining sessions and has its home link in the mobile network. A Visiting Mobile Node can also move, but its home link lies outside the network.

A mobile network becomes nested when another mobile network attaches to it. The upstream network is the parent-NEMO; the attached downstream network is a sub-NEMO. The top of the hierarchy is the root-NEMO, connected to the fixed Internet through a root-MR. The RFC defines depth by counting the sub-MRs a packet crosses between a node and the root-MR.
sections.plainLanguage: Nodes differ by whether they can move and whether their home link is inside the mobile network. One mobile network can also attach through another, creating parent, child, and root roles.

sections.title: Multihoming and Split Networks
sections.content:
A host or mobile-network node is multihomed when it has several addresses to choose from, because it has multiple prefixes or interfaces. A mobile router can be multihomed for the same reasons, and a mobile network can be multihomed if it has a multihomed router or multiple routers available.

A nested mobile network is multihomed when it has multiple root-MRs or a multihomed root-MR. A Split-NEMO occurs when mobile routers that handle the same mobile-network prefix separate, leaving two or more independent mobile networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Multihoming means a host or network has more than one address or route to choose from. A Split-NEMO is a network that separates into independent networks while its routers handle the same prefix.

sections.title: Mobility Support and Routing
sections.content:
Host Mobility Support maintains sessions when a mobile host changes its point of attachment. Network Mobility Support aims to maintain sessions for nodes behind a mobile router when that router moves. The RFC divides network support into Basic and Extended support.

NEMO Basic Support uses bidirectional tunnels between mobile routers and their home agents, without route optimization; RFC 3963 specifies the solution. NEMO Extended Support covers performance optimizations, including route optimization. The RFC also names an MRHA tunnel between a mobile router and its home agent and a pinball route, where packets pass through one or more home agents instead of taking a direct path.
sections.plainLanguage: Basic NEMO support sends traffic through a tunnel between the mobile router and its home agent. The RFC uses pinball route for an indirect path that passes through one or more home agents.

viz.caption: THREE FUNCTIONAL ROLES FOR NODES IN A MOBILE NETWORK

items.title: Local Fixed Node
items.text: Belongs to the mobile network and cannot move while keeping sessions.

items.title: Local Mobile Node
items.text: Can move while keeping sessions; its home link is in the mobile network.

items.title: Visiting Mobile Node
items.text: Can move while keeping sessions; its home link is outside the mobile network.
